records.place: Franschhoek, in the valley's southern corner, Franschhoek district, Coastal Region

wine.name: Boekenhoutskloof Syrah
wine.grapes: Syrah, all of it, a share of each vintage fermented as whole bunches.
wine.sites: Mostly Porseleinberg, the house's farm near Riebeek-Kasteel in the Swartland, its vines in decomposed mica schist, with the rest from the Goldmine vineyard, also in the Swartland; none of the fruit is grown in Franschhoek.
wine.making: The grapes are chilled in a cold room, then fermented spontaneously in tulip shaped concrete tanks, with a share of whole bunches that varies by year, little sulphur and no added acid, the cap worked by délestage. The wine is pressed and moved by gravity into large Austrian oak foudres and demi-muids, where it rests for up to eighteen months.
wine.glass: Violet, white pepper and blackberry over smoked meat and black olive, perfumed rather than heavy, with fine, polished tannin, fresh acidity and a savoury, stony finish.
wine.ageing: Approachable within a few years of release for its fine tannin, it gains savoury depth over a decade and more in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour to open its perfume; a large Syrah or Burgundy glass.

label.means: Certified under the Cape's Wine of Origin scheme as grown in the Swartland, though the wine is made in Franschhoek.
Afrikaans for the ravine of the boekenhout, the Cape beech, a native tree once prized for furniture.
The grape the Cape also calls Shiraz; the house prints Syrah on this label.

records.table: Boekenhoutskloof Syrah is made in Franschhoek from Swartland fruit, mostly the house's own Porseleinberg farm, fermented wild in concrete with whole bunches and aged in large foudres. It is perfumed and peppery rather than heavy, so pour it with lamb or game.
records.story: The farm in the southern corner of the Franschhoek valley dates, by the house's account, to 1776, and takes its name from the boekenhout, the Cape beech, a native tree prized by the Cape's furniture makers; the seven chairs on the label recall that craft. In 1993 a group of partners, its winemaker among them, bought the run down farm and homestead, restored them and began a new vineyard programme. The first Syrah came with the 1997 vintage, and it is credited with establishing Syrah as a serious Cape variety and the house as its specialist. The search for Syrah grapes of that quality led the house in 2009 to buy Porseleinberg, a farm near Riebeek-Kasteel in the Swartland, and Porseleinberg fruit, with some from the Goldmine vineyard, has since made most of the wine, which carries Wine of Origin Swartland. Porseleinberg also gives a Syrah under its own name, a separate label. The valley's own wine of the house is white: Sémillon from old bush vines on the Franschhoek riverbed, planted in 1902 and 1942, with a block of 1936 beside them. Boekenhoutskloof Syrah teaches a sommelier that a Cape label names where the grapes grow, never the cellar's address.

others.name: Boekenhoutskloof Semillon
others.note: The valley's own wine of the house, from old vines on the Franschhoek riverbed planted in 1902, 1936 and 1942.

others.name: The Chocolate Block
others.note: A Syrah led Cape red blend and the house's widest known wine; a dry red, with no chocolate in it.

others.name: Boekenhoutskloof Cabernet Sauvignon
others.note: Firm, cedary Cape Cabernet drawn largely from Stellenbosch fruit.

traps: Boekenhoutskloof Syrah is made in Franschhoek, but its fruit is the Swartland's, so its label carries Wine of Origin Swartland, not Franschhoek.
Porseleinberg is the house's Swartland farm and a separate label of its own; Boekenhoutskloof Syrah draws on its fruit but is a different wine.
The Chocolate Block is a dry red blend led by Syrah, not a sweet wine and not flavoured with chocolate.

cards.front: Boekenhoutskloof Syrah: which farm gives most of its fruit, and where does it lie?
cards.back: Porseleinberg, near Riebeek-Kasteel in the Swartland, bought by the house in 2009.

cards.front: What do the seven chairs on a Boekenhoutskloof label recall?
cards.back: The Cape's furniture craft, and the boekenhout, the Cape beech whose wood was prized for it.

Franschhoek was a ward of the Swartland until 2010

report: The house's own pages disagree on the purchase: one says the farm and homestead were bought and restored in 1993, another that a group of friends bought it in 1996; the library and a secondary source give 1993, which the record keeps.

The Wine of Origin Swartland rests on Berry Bros, Decanter and a critic's listings of the 2016 to 2023 vintages; Decanter lists the 2012 as Wine of Origin Coastal Region with fruit largely from Wellington, a fact left out of the record for want of a second source.
The 1997 fruit is told as bought fruit by one source and as a Somerset West vineyard by another, so the record says nothing of where it grew.
The glass and the ageing are the author's reading of the library's style line (perfumed, peppery, polished tannin) and review summaries; no stated drinking window was found.
The library's country field for this house reads Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and South America, a sheet label rather than a country; the record treats it as South Africa.
No swap proposed: the Syrah is the house's flagship in every source read, and the merge read's rule is followed, the Sémillon named in others as the valley's own wine of the house.

records.place: Franschhoek, on the Franschhoek Pass above the village, Franschhoek district

wine.name: Pierre Jourdan Brut
wine.classification: Cap Classique, the Cape's name for bottle fermented sparkling wine
wine.grapes: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir alone, Chardonnay the larger part.
wine.sites: By the house's account, grapes grown on Cabrière itself, on the slopes of the Franschhoek Pass above the village, and only the cuvée, the first and gentlest pressing, is used.
wine.making: Made by the traditional method: the cuvée of Chardonnay and Pinot Noir becomes a still base wine, which is bottled with yeast and sugar for its second fermentation, aged on its lees, riddled and disgorged, then finished brut. The house speaks of extended lees ageing but gives no figure in the notes read.
wine.glass: Delicate brioche and citrus blossom over fresh lemon and yeasty notes, with a fine mousse, crisp acidity and a subtle, chalky finish.
wine.ageing: Released ready to drink as a non vintage wine, it is at its freshest within a few years of release.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a tulip or white wine glass rather than a narrow flute.

label.means: The name the house gives its Cap Classique wines, after the Huguenot granted the farm in 1694.
The Cape's term for sparkling wine given its second fermentation in the bottle.
Dry, with little sugar added after disgorgement.

records.table: Pierre Jourdan Brut is Haute Cabrière's Cap Classique, named for the Huguenot granted the farm in 1694: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir from the house's Franschhoek slopes, fermented a second time in the bottle. It tastes of brioche and citrus blossom, so pour it cold as an aperitif.
records.story: On 22 December 1694 the land on the slope above what became the village of Franschhoek was granted to Pierre Jourdan, a Huguenot farmer who had fled France, and the farm took the name Cabrière. Its modern life began with a winemaker who, as cellar master at Boschendal, had made that estate's first Cap Classique in 1981, which made Boschendal the second producer of the style in the Cape after Simonsig. In the early 1980s he settled on Cabrière to make sparkling wine of his own from Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, the grapes of Champagne, and by the house's account Pierre Jourdan Brut was created in 1984 and released in 1986, the first wine of the cellar. The house set a rule it has kept since: its Cap Classique wines carry the name of the Huguenot, Pierre Jourdan, and its still wines the name of the farm, Haute Cabrière. A cellar, a tasting room and a restaurant were later cut into the mountainside on the Franschhoek Pass, cool in summer. The founder, mourned across the Cape trade as a pioneer of Cap Classique, died in December 2025. Pierre Jourdan Brut is the wine to know as the valley's sparkling signature, the bridge between Boschendal's early bottles and the many Cap Classique houses of Franschhoek.

others.name: Pierre Jourdan Blanc de Blancs
others.note: A Chardonnay Cap Classique given far longer on its lees than the Brut.

others.name: Haute Cabrière Pinot Noir Réserve
others.note: A still Pinot Noir, carrying the farm's name as all the house's still wines do.

traps: Haute Cabrière's sparkling wines carry the name Pierre Jourdan and its still wines the name Haute Cabrière; Pierre Jourdan is not a separate estate.
Pierre Jourdan Brut was not the Cape's first Cap Classique: Simonsig made the first, and Boschendal, under the same founder, the second, in 1981.

cards.front: Haute Cabrière: which name goes on its Cap Classique, and which on its still wines?
cards.back: Pierre Jourdan, the Huguenot granted the farm in 1694, on the Cap Classique; Haute Cabrière on the still wines.

cards.front: Where had the founder of Haute Cabrière made Cap Classique before?
cards.back: At Boschendal, as cellar master, where he made the estate's first in 1981.

questions.q: A guest asks which grapes make Pierre Jourdan Brut. Which answer fits?
opts: Chenin Blanc with a little Chardonnay
questions.exp: The house makes Pierre Jourdan Brut from Chardonnay and Pinot Noir only, Chardonnay the larger part; it uses no Meunier and no Chenin Blanc.

questions.q: On which date, by the house's account, was the Haute Cabrière land granted to Pierre Jourdan?
questions.exp: The house dates the grant to 22 December 1694; 1688 is the year the Huguenots began to settle the valley, and 1794 is a century too late.

report: The founder, Achim von Arnim, died on 8 December 2025 aged 80 by Winemag and the South African government news agency, but his year of birth was not found in two sources, so he is described and never named; the Winemag address carries his name, and he is dead, so it stands.

The first release: the house's shop page says the wine was created in 1984, its blog that it was the cellar's first release in 1986, and Wikipedia and a second secondary source give 1986; the record tells both as the house's account.

The year the founder settled on Cabrière is 1982 in one article and the 1980s in Wikipedia, so the record says the early 1980s. The cellar's opening on 22 December 1994, three hundred years after the grant, rests on one source and is left out.
The claim of the first Cap Classique made wholly from Chardonnay and Pinot Noir rests on one source and is left out.

The Wine of Origin is a doubt: a critic's tasting site lists the non vintage Brut as Western Cape, while the house's note on wine.co.za says it is made solely from Cabrière fruit, which would allow Franschhoek; the record keeps Western Cape and the checker should confirm it on a label.
The blend is 60 per cent Chardonnay on one sheet and 85 per cent on another, so the record says Chardonnay the larger part; no lees time for the Brut was found.
Pierre Jourdan's own dates and his home village in France were not found in two sources, so he carries none; he is named because the wine bears his name.

records.place: Groot Drakenstein, at the mouth of the Franschhoek valley, Western Cape

wine.name: Grande Cuvée Brut
wine.classification: Cap Classique, the Cape's name for bottle fermented sparkling wine
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay in roughly equal parts, the balance moving from vintage to vintage.
wine.sites: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir from the cool Elgin district of the Cape South Coast, not from the home farm in the Franschhoek valley.
wine.making: Made by the traditional method as a vintage wine: the base wine is bottled with yeast and sugar for its second fermentation, then aged on its lees for at least three years before it is riddled, disgorged and given a brut dosage, which builds the creamy texture the house seeks.
wine.glass: Fresh green apple and lemon over almond biscotti and brioche, with a full, creamy mousse from its long time on the lees and a long, seamless finish.
wine.ageing: Ready to drink on release after its years on the lees, a good vintage keeps for some years more.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a tulip or white wine glass to show its brioche.

label.means: The house's vintage Cap Classique, aged longer on its lees than its non vintage Brut.
Certified under the Cape's scheme as grown in the cool Elgin district of the Cape South Coast.
Dry, with little sugar added after disgorgement.

records.table: Boschendal Grande Cuvée Brut is the vintage Cap Classique of one of the Cape's old farms: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay from cool Elgin, aged at least three years on its lees. It tastes of green apple, almond and brioche, creamy and long, so serve it cold.
records.story: Boschendal dates its beginning to 1685, when Jean le Long, a French Huguenot, is said to have been granted the land; other accounts put the grant in 1688 and the title deed in 1713. In 1715 the farm was bought by Abraham de Villiers, and his family kept it for 164 years, until 1879. In 1897, in most accounts, the mining magnate Cecil John Rhodes (1853 to 1902) bought it among the farms he gathered in the valley to grow fruit, and it became part of Rhodes Fruit Farms. In 1969 Anglo American took a majority of that company, renamed Anglo American Farms, and held Boschendal until a sale to a consortium of investors in 2003. In 1981 the estate's cellar master made its first Cap Classique, a vintage Brut, and Boschendal became the second producer of the style in the Cape after Simonsig. That cellar master went on to found Haute Cabrière, higher up the same valley. The Grande Cuvée Brut is the house's vintage expression of that tradition, drawn from Elgin and rested at least three years on its lees before release. To a sommelier it shows a Franschhoek valley house of more than three centuries that reaches to a cooler district for its sparkling fruit.

others.name: Boschendal Brut
others.note: The non vintage Cap Classique of Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, the house's everyday sparkling wine.

others.name: Boschendal Elgin Chardonnay
others.note: A still Chardonnay from the same cool district as the Grande Cuvée.

traps: Grande Cuvée Brut carries Wine of Origin Elgin: its fruit does not grow on the Franschhoek valley farm where Boschendal stands.
Boschendal was the Cape's second producer of Cap Classique, from 1981; Simonsig in Stellenbosch made the first.

cards.front: Boschendal Grande Cuvée Brut: where does its fruit grow?
cards.back: In the cool Elgin district of the Cape South Coast, so it carries Wine of Origin Elgin.

cards.front: Which family held Boschendal for 164 years from 1715?

questions.exp: The house ages the Grande Cuvée on its lees for at least three years, which gives its brioche and creamy mousse; six months would be far too short for a bottle fermented vintage wine.

questions.q: Who bought Boschendal in 1897, in most accounts, to grow fruit?
questions.exp: Rhodes gathered fruit farms in the valley, Boschendal among them; Abraham de Villiers bought it in 1715, and Anglo American came in only in 1969.

report: The pick was in doubt; the house's own pages and menus read set no single wine at the head of the range, and no Cecil John Reserve Shiraz label was found, so the Grande Cuvée Brut is kept as the house's vintage Cap Classique, the style that made its name from 1981.

The grant: 1685 is the house's date (SA History Online, and a 2026 house piece on 340 years); Wikipedia gives a grant of 1688 and a title deed of 1713. The record tells both, so founded keeps 1685 as the house's year.

Rhodes's purchase is 1897 in SA History Online and in Wikipedia's account of March 1897, but 1887 in another Wikipedia line, so it is told as 1897 in most accounts; his dates rest on Britannica and Wikipedia, read in search but not listed for the cap of five sources.

Anglo American's year is 1969 in Wikipedia and Engineering News but 1987 in one source; the sale is 2003 in the Mail and Guardian and Wikipedia, 2004 in one other. Later sales of 2005 and 2012 are left out.

The Wine of Origin Elgin rests on Decanter's Elgin listings of the 2012 and 2020 and an IWSC entry; one retailer lists the 2016 as Stellenbosch. The lees time of at least 36 months rests on a trade listing and a house article; the varietal split moves by vintage.
One account gives the maiden Brut of 1981 as Crouchen Blanc, Shiraz and Tinta Barocca, with Pinot Noir from 1982 and Chardonnay from 1985; it rests on one source and is left out.
Jean le Long and Abraham de Villiers carry no dates, since none were found in two sources.

wine.name: Pierneef Syrah Viognier
wine.grapes: Syrah, the great majority, with a small share of Viognier fermented together with it.
wine.sites: Syrah from cool sites near the south coast, mostly Elim, with Walker Bay and, from 2018, Napier, and some Franschhoek Syrah in earlier years; the Viognier is from Franschhoek, chosen because it ripens late enough to pick with the Syrah.
wine.making: The grapes are sorted by hand and destemmed, and the Franschhoek Viognier, picked with the Syrah, is fermented with it, with regular pump overs and two to four weeks on the skins. Free run and press wine go together into French oak barrels of three hundred litres, part of them new, for about eighteen months before bottling.
wine.glass: Black cherry, plum and white pepper lifted by a floral, apricot edge from the Viognier, smooth and medium to full in body, with ripe, supple tannin and a savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Open and generous within a few years of release, it gains savoury depth over the following decade.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a large Syrah glass.

label.means: The house's range named for the painter Jacob Hendrik Pierneef, its labels reproducing his linocuts.
The name the wine carries from the 2020 vintage on: the same Syrah and Viognier under a new label.
The origin a blend of more than one Cape district carries, here the south coast and Franschhoek.

records.table: La Motte's Pierneef Syrah Viognier is cool coastal Syrah, mostly from Elim, fermented with a little Franschhoek Viognier and aged in French oak, its label carrying a linocut by the painter Pierneef. Expect dark cherry and pepper with a floral lift; serve it with lamb.
records.story: The land was granted in 1695 to Hans Hendrik Hattingh, a German settler, and in 1709 it was bought by Pierre Joubert, the farm's first Huguenot owner, who named it after La Motte d'Aigues, a village in Provence. In 1970 the industrialist Anton Rupert (1916 to 2006) bought La Motte and restored it, and the old cellar, once its renovation was done, was declared a national monument in December 1975. The Rupert family also gathered a large private collection of the work of Jacob Hendrik Pierneef (1886 to 1957), the painter of the South African landscape, and in 2009 the estate acquired a heritage collection of his work from his daughter; it is shown in the museum on the estate. The Pierneef wines followed in the early 2000s, their labels reproducing his linocuts, made with his family's leave since his copyright still stood. The Syrah Viognier turned to cool coastal Syrah, chiefly from Elim, fermented with Viognier from the valley, and from the 2020 vintage it carries the name Pierneef Atelier. To a sommelier it is a Franschhoek house's red grown mostly far from Franschhoek, and an estate where wine, painting and history share the same ground.

others.name: La Motte Syrah
others.note: The estate's own Syrah, released beside the Pierneef in the same years.

others.name: Pierneef Sauvignon Blanc

traps: Pierneef Syrah Viognier is grown mostly at Elim and elsewhere near the south coast, not in Franschhoek; only the Viognier, and in some years a little Syrah, is the valley's.
From the 2020 vintage the wine is labelled Pierneef Atelier: the same Syrah and Viognier, not a new wine.
The Viognier is fermented with the Syrah, in the manner of Côte-Rôtie, not blended in after the barrels.

Made into a separate sweet wine
Kept apart to refresh the barrels

questions.q: Who bought La Motte in 1970 and restored it?
questions.exp: Anton Rupert bought La Motte in 1970 and restored it; Pierre Joubert bought the farm in 1709 and named it after a Provençal village.

report: The pick holds the plan's words, but from the 2020 vintage the house sells the wine as Pierneef Atelier (its own release note and two retailers); the record keeps the plan's name, says so in label and traps, and the integrator may wish to rename it as other batches did. Hanneli R, named for a living member of the family, sits above it and is not named.

The Wine of Origin Western Cape is inferred, not seen on a label: the house's sheets give Syrah from Elim, Walker Bay and Napier with Franschhoek Viognier, and under the scheme a blend across the Cape South Coast and the Coastal Region can carry only Western Cape. Decanter files the 2013 under Franschhoek, which the sheets contradict; the checker should confirm.

The plan's why speaks of a farm of the late seventeenth century known for Shiraz and Sauvignon Blanc; the house's history gives a German settler's grant of 1695 and the Huguenot Joubert's purchase of 1709, so the Huguenot name dates from 1709.

Pierneef's dates (1886 to 1957) rest on the house's own museum pages, read in search; the Pierneef range's start is early 2002 in one source and is told as the early 2000s. The first vintage of the Syrah Viognier seen on the house's sheets is 2004.
Anton Rupert's dates rest on Wikipedia and the Mail and Guardian; the cellar's monument status of December 1975 on the house's history and one other.
The glass and the ageing are the author's reading; no review summary of the Syrah Viognier's taste was read, so the checker may trim them.
The making's barrel time is about eighteen months by the house's sheets (fourteen months, then about four after blending; eighteen in 2018; twenty four in 2020 for a delayed bottling).

wine.name: Reserve Chardonnay
wine.sites: A single block on the estate, planted in the mid 1980s by the house's lists, on the cool, south west facing slopes of the Franschhoek mountains, where the farm's vines climb from about four hundred metres.
wine.making: Fermented in barrel and matured in oak, with a share of the wine made in concrete eggs for texture beside the barrels. The wine is blended and bottled after its time in wood and released in the second year after the harvest.
wine.glass: Lemon butter, green apple and buttered toast, with dried pineapple, honey and beeswax in riper years, held by a cool line of acidity and a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Taut when young, it opens after two or three years in bottle and keeps for a decade in a good vintage.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius; no need to decant, though air helps a young bottle; a Burgundy white glass.

label.means: The house's name for its single block Chardonnay, above the estate Chardonnay.
Grown in the Franschhoek district, a ward of Paarl until 2010.

records.table: Chamonix Reserve Chardonnay comes from a single block planted in the 1980s high on the Franschhoek mountain slopes, fermented in barrel with a little made in concrete eggs. It tastes of lemon butter, green apple and toast with a cool line of acidity.
records.story: Chamonix was once part of La Cotte, one of the Huguenot farms of the valley, whose history the house traces to 1688. The farm took its present name from the Alpine town in France, and by the early 1990s it had been bought by a German born businessman; the house dates its founding as a wine farm to 1991, at the start of a new era for Cape wine as the country opened to the world. The estate lies against the mountain on cool, south west facing slopes, and its vineyards are among the higher of the valley, which gives the house its name for Chardonnay and Pinot Noir of freshness rather than weight. Its oldest vines, by the house's account, are a block of Chenin Blanc planted in 1965, and the Reserve Chardonnay comes from a single block planted in the mid 1980s. The house ferments it in barrel, with a share in concrete eggs, and holds it back until the second year after the harvest. In the Cape the Reserve Chardonnay and the Reserve Pinot Noir are the wines Chamonix is known by. To a sommelier the Reserve Chardonnay shows what height and a cool mountain aspect give Franschhoek: Chardonnay of tension and lemon freshness in a valley better known for its Sémillon and its sparkling wine.

others.name: Chamonix Reserve Pinot Noir
others.note: The house's Pinot Noir, often named beside the Chardonnay as its signature.

others.name: Chamonix Old Vine Steen
others.note: Chenin Blanc from the farm's block planted in 1965.

others.name: Chamonix Chardonnay
others.note: The estate Chardonnay, matured in small French barrels.

traps: Chamonix in Franschhoek is a Cape wine farm named after the French Alpine town; it has nothing to do with the wines of Savoie.
The Reserve Chardonnay is an estate wine from one block on the farm, not bought fruit from Elgin or another cool district; its label carries Wine of Origin Franschhoek.

cards.front: Which historic Huguenot farm was Chamonix once part of?

questions.q: A guest asks where Chamonix Reserve Chardonnay grows. Which answer fits?

Bought fruit from across the Cape South Coast
Old bush vines on the Franschhoek riverbed
The cool Elgin valley beyond the mountains

questions.q: In which year does Chamonix date its founding as a wine farm?
questions.exp: The house dates its founding to 1991; 1688 is the date of La Cotte, the Huguenot farm it was once part of, and 1965 that of its oldest Chenin Blanc.

report: The owner who bought the farm in the early 1990s is named on the house's page; whether he is living was not settled, so he is described and never named. The purchase is 1990 in one source and the early nineties in another; the house's page gives the founding as 1991, which founded keeps.

The renaming from Waterval to Chamonix in 1965 by a family named Pickering, and the farm's past as an export fruit farm, each rest on one source and are left out, so the story says only that it took the name of the Alpine town.

The block's planting in the mid 1980s rests on vine ages of 27 years in 2011 (a critic's note, read in search but not listed) and 29 years in the house's lists of 2013 and 2014; the house's 2016 list gives 36 years, which does not agree, and the checker may cut the date to the block alone.
The share in concrete eggs is 20 per cent in the house's list and 10 per cent in one review, so the record says a share; the barrel time of about fourteen months rests on one review and is left out.

Whether the Reserve Chardonnay or the Reserve Pinot Noir is the house's flagship is open: one source calls the Pinot Noir the signature, others the Chardonnay a strength; no swap is proposed, but the checker may weigh a swap to the Reserve Pinot Noir. Troika, the plan's Bordeaux blend, was not confirmed and is not named.

The long serving winemaker who left in 2015 is living and rests on one source, so he is left out; the glass draws on Decanter's 2015 and Wine Advocate's 2014 notes as summarised in search, and the ageing is the author's reading.
